intro: OpenVAT started as a way to bake Blender animation into textures. It’s also a Unity system for bringing those animations into a project and controlling them in gameplay.
origamiTitle: The animation is in the texture.
origamiText: OpenVAT records the evaluated mesh, frame by frame. A shader reads that motion back as vertex offsets, so the engine doesn’t need to reproduce the original rig, modifier stack, or simulation.
origamiNote: This folding example shows the same animation as texture data, vertex offsets, and the final mesh. It’s a useful way to see what the texture is actually doing.
explainer: Each vertex gets a location in a texture, and time runs through the frames. The values stored there describe how the mesh moves. Playback happens on the GPU.
features: I built the baking around Blender’s evaluated geometry. If a modifier, Geometry Nodes setup, or rig deforms the mesh, OpenVAT can capture the result.
Normals and custom per-vertex attributes can be encoded too. That gives a shader more to work with than a single position animation.
The texture holds the data; a shader decides how to use it. Timing, per-instance offsets, masks, and blending can make the same bake useful in different ways.
work: I built both sides of the workflow: a Blender encoder driven by Geometry Nodes and Python, and a Unity receiver with import, shader, and playback tools. Building them together meant working through the practical details too: vertex mapping, normals, precision, and engine import settings.
limit: The mesh needs stable topology: the vertex count and order must stay consistent through the animation. The motion itself is baked; playback and other runtime behavior depend on the engine integration and shader.
